children.text: Nifty closes at 26,500 on Monday. By Wednesday morning, it has dropped to 26,150 on weak global cues. A junior analyst plots the 26,100 strike's IV on both days, sees it jumped from 14.6% to something noticeably higher, and reports that 'the smile got steeper.' It did not. The strike that was 1.5% out of the money on Monday is almost exactly at the money on Wednesday. The IV moved because the desk was reading the wrong axis, not because the market's view of skew changed.

body.text: Raw strike is a spot-dependent coordinate, so a smile plotted against strike appears to move every time spot moves, even if nothing about relative skew has changed. Desks instead parametrize the surface in moneyness, log-moneyness or delta, coordinates that stay meaningful as spot drifts.

children.text: Why Strike Is the Wrong Coordinate

body.caption: The same strike, read on two different days, looks like a different point on the curve

body.text: Nothing about the shape of the skew needs to have changed between Monday and Wednesday for that IV to fall. The 26,100 strike simply migrated from a 1.5% OTM put, sitting higher up the put wing, to almost exactly at the money, sitting near the bottom of the curve where IV is lowest. Comparing raw IV at a fixed strike across two different spot levels compares two different points on the smile, not the same point twice.

markDefs.definition: The price at which you could contractually lock in buying or selling the underlying at a future date, F = S·e^(rT), ignoring dividends. It is the natural centre point for a volatility smile, not spot itself.

children.text: The standard fix is to stop plotting IV against strike and start plotting it against log-moneyness, k = ln(K / F), where F is the
. A strike that is always 1.5% below the forward always has the same k, on any day, at any spot level, which is exactly the property raw strike lacks.

body.caption: Forward price and log-moneyness. Desks quote smiles against k rather than K precisely so the curve looks the same day to day when the underlying's relative skew hasn't changed.

body.title: Computing the forward price
body.prompt: Nifty spot is 26,500, the risk-free rate is 6.5%, and time to expiry is 30/365 years. Using F = S·e^(rT), what is the forward price, to the nearest whole rupee?
body.explanation: rT = 0.065 × 30/365 ≈ 0.005343. e^0.005343 ≈ 1.005357. F = 26,500 × 1.005357 ≈ 26,642. Every strike's log-moneyness in this expiry is measured against this forward, not against the 26,500 spot.

children.text: Delta as a Coordinate: The 25-Delta Convention

markDefs.definition: A quoting convention borrowed from FX and interest rate vol desks, where strikes are identified by their Black-Scholes delta, such as the 25-delta put or the 10-delta call, instead of by their strike price. The ATM point, 25-delta put, and 25-delta call together form the standard three-point 'risk reversal and butterfly' quote used across Chapter 2.

children.text: Vol desks go one step further and index the smile by

, not strike or even log-moneyness. Delta already blends together strike, spot, volatility and time into a single number that has an intuitive reading, roughly the probability the option expires in the money. A '25-delta put' is not a fixed strike, it is whichever strike currently has a Black-Scholes put delta of −0.25, and that strike is re-solved every time spot or IV moves.

body.label: The 25,700 put from Chapter 1's chain example, in delta terms
body.context: Using S = 26,500, K = 25,700, IV = 16.8%, T = 30/365, r = 6.5% from the previous lesson's chain: d1 ≈ 0.771, so N(d1) ≈ 0.780 and put delta = N(d1) − 1 ≈ −0.220. This strike sits close to, but not exactly on, the standard 25-delta point desks quote around.

body.code:
from scipy.optimize import brentq
from scipy.stats import norm
import numpy as np

def bs_delta(S, K, T, r, sigma, option_type):
    d1 = (np.log(S / K) + (r + 0.5 * sigma ** 2) * T) / (sigma * np.sqrt(T))
    if option_type == "call":
        return norm.cdf(d1)
    return norm.cdf(d1) - 1

def strike_for_target_delta(target_delta, S, T, r, sigma, option_type):
    # Solve for the strike whose BS delta equals target_delta,
    # e.g. target_delta = -0.25 for the 25-delta put
    objective = lambda K: bs_delta(S, K, T, r, sigma, option_type) - target_delta
    return brentq(objective, S * 0.5, S * 1.5)

S, T, r, sigma = 26500, 30 / 365, 0.065, 0.155
k25_put = strike_for_target_delta(-0.25, S, T, r, sigma, "put")
k25_call = strike_for_target_delta(0.25, S, T, r, sigma, "call")
print(f"25-delta put strike: {k25_put:.0f}, 25-delta call strike: {k25_call:.0f}")
body.caption: Inverting delta instead of price: solving for the strike that produces a target Black-Scholes delta, the building block for quoting a smile in delta space

children.text: Choosing a coordinate is not just cosmetic. It embeds an assumption about how the whole surface moves when spot moves, and that assumption changes what your hedge actually does.

body.title: Two ways the surface can move with spot

columns.label: Sticky strike
points: IV at each fixed absolute strike stays the same as spot moves
The smile does not translate; it sits still in strike space
A strike's 'moneyness label' effectively changes as spot passes through it
Matches a market where option prices barely react to spot moves beyond what delta alone predicts

columns.label: Sticky delta (sticky moneyness)
points: IV at each fixed delta or moneyness stays the same as spot moves
The whole smile shifts along with spot, riding the new forward
A given strike's IV changes purely because spot moved past it
Matches a market where the shape of relative skew is stable but its centre tracks spot

body.text: Under a sticky-delta market, a fall in spot pushes what used to be a middling OTM put strike closer to the money, and since the smile is downward sloping in skew terms, that strike's IV rises purely because of where it now sits on the curve, not because anything fundamental changed. That spot-driven change in IV at a fixed strike is precisely what the second-order Greek Vanna measures and prices. Chapter 4 gives it a formal treatment; for now, recognise that your choice of sticky-strike or sticky-delta assumption changes how much of a spot move you expect to show up as a change in option value through the vega channel, not just the delta channel.

body.title: Reading a fixed-strike IV change
body.question: Nifty spot falls 2% overnight. A trader observes that the IV of a specific OTM put strike, unchanged in absolute terms, has risen noticeably. Assuming the underlying market is behaving in a broadly sticky-delta way, what is the most likely explanation?
options: The strike is now closer to the money on the downward-sloping skew, so it inherits a higher IV even though relative skew is unchanged
NSE has widened the strike interval overnight
The risk-free rate used in the pricing model must have increased sharply
This can only happen if the option's open interest fell to zero
body.explanation: In a sticky-delta regime, the smile's shape in moneyness or delta terms is roughly stable, so it is expected to shift bodily as spot moves. A strike that was further out of the money becomes relatively closer to the money after a spot drop, and since the skew rises toward lower strikes, that strike picks up higher IV purely from its new position on the curve. Strike intervals, the risk-free rate and open interest are unrelated to this mechanism.

children.text: Fitting a Smooth Surface: A First Look at SVI

A chain only lists a finite set of strikes. If you need the IV at a strike NSE doesn't list, for a custom delta target, for a risk report, or to price an OTC-style structure, you need a continuous curve, not a handful of discrete points. Simply drawing straight lines between the solved IVs works badly: linear interpolation on IV can quietly create a tiny arbitrage in the implied option prices, since it does not respect how variance, not volatility, actually needs to behave across strikes. The standard fix is to fit a smooth parametric curve to the discrete points and interpolate on that instead.

markDefs.definition: Implied volatility squared, multiplied by time to expiry: w(k, T) = σ(k, T)² · T. Vol surfaces are fitted and interpolated in total variance space, not raw volatility space, because it behaves more predictably across both strike and time.

children.text: The most widely used parametric form in practice is Gatheral's raw SVI, 'stochastic volatility inspired', which fits
as a function of log-moneyness with five parameters.

body.caption: Gatheral's raw SVI parametrization of total implied variance w(k) = IV² · T against log-moneyness k
The five SVI parameters, read intuitively

cells: Shifts the whole curve up or down; roughly the base variance level
How fast variance rises moving away from the centre on either wing; b ≥ 0
Tilts the curve so one wing rises faster than the other; −1 < ρ < 1, negative for the typical equity index put skew
Moves the location of the curve's minimum along the log-moneyness axis
Controls how sharply rounded or V-shaped the bottom of the curve is; σ > 0

body.text: A fitted curve is only useful if it is arbitrage-free. Two conditions matter in practice: total variance must not decrease as expiry lengthens for the same k, otherwise you could construct a calendar spread that is free money, and the implied probability density the curve produces must stay non-negative everywhere, otherwise you could construct a butterfly that is free money. Checking and enforcing both is a real engineering problem on any production surface, and it is beyond what this lesson covers in full, but knowing the two failure modes by name is what lets you sanity-check a fitted curve before trusting it.

body.title: Pricing an unlisted delta
body.scenario: Your desk needs the IV at the 15-delta put for risk reporting, but NSE's listed strikes on this expiry only bracket it, one strike solves to a 12-delta put and the next solves to a 19-delta put. A colleague suggests just averaging the two IVs since 15 sits roughly between 12 and 19.
body.prompt: Is straight-line averaging between the two neighbouring IVs a reasonable way to get the 15-delta IV? What would you do instead?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Linear interpolation directly on IV, or even on delta-to-IV in a naive straight line, is not guaranteed to respect the true convexity of the smile and can introduce small arbitrage into the interpolated point, especially if the two bracketing points are far apart on the curve.
2. The more robust approach is to fit a smooth arbitrage-checked curve, such as raw SVI, to all the available listed strikes on this expiry first, in total variance versus log-moneyness space, not raw IV versus delta.
3. Convert the target 15-delta point to its corresponding log-moneyness (via a delta-to-strike solve, as in the code above, then strike to log-moneyness), read the fitted curve's total variance at that k, and convert back to an implied volatility.
4. This respects the actual shape of the curve between the two listed points instead of assuming it is a straight line, and it is consistent with how every other point on the surface, listed or not, is being read.
5. If the fit ever looks unstable with only two nearby points, the honest answer is to flag the interpolated number as low-confidence rather than reporting it with false precision, since a two-point SVI fit is barely constrained.

cards.definition: F = S·e^(rT), the natural centre point for a volatility smile, distinct from spot.
k = ln(K/F). A spot-independent coordinate for comparing the same relative point on a smile across different days.
Quoting a strike by its Black-Scholes delta, such as a 25-delta put, instead of by its strike price, blending spot, strike, vol and time into one intuitive number.
The assumption that IV at each fixed absolute strike stays constant as spot moves, so the smile itself does not translate.
The assumption that IV at each fixed delta or moneyness stays constant as spot moves, so the whole smile shifts to track the new forward.
Gatheral's five-parameter parametric curve fitting total implied variance against log-moneyness, used to interpolate and extrapolate a smooth, checkable smile from discrete listed strikes.

points: Raw strike is a spot-dependent coordinate; comparing a fixed strike's IV across two different spot levels compares two different points on the smile, not the same point twice.
Log-moneyness, k = ln(K/F), and delta are the standard spot-independent coordinates desks use to plot and compare smiles day to day.
A '25-delta put' is the strike whose Black-Scholes delta currently equals −0.25, re-solved continuously, not a fixed strike price.

Sticky strike assumes IV is pinned to absolute strikes; sticky delta assumes IV is pinned to moneyness or delta and the smile rides along with spot. The distinction directly affects how spot moves flow into option values through vega, previewing Vanna in Chapter 4.

Discrete, listed-strike IVs should be interpolated and extrapolated through a smooth, arbitrage-checked parametric fit, such as raw SVI in total variance space, not by drawing straight lines between IV points.
The two arbitrage conditions to know by name are calendar arbitrage, variance decreasing with time, and butterfly arbitrage, a negative implied density.
